title: Agentic Security: When AI Becomes Both Defender and Threat
takeaways: Introduces the concept of Agentic Security, where autonomous AI serves dual roles as a protective measure and a potential security risk.
Examines key cybersecurity paradigms for autonomous systems, specifically focusing on trust, control, and resilience.
Serves as an introductory student guide to understanding modern AI-driven threat landscapes and defense mechanisms.

title: It's not who can build now, it is who you trust - From Creator to Curator Economy
takeaways: The competitive differentiator in AI has shifted from technical building capability to trust and reliability.
The technology landscape is transitioning from a Creator Economy toward a Curator Economy centered on trusted oversight.

title: Agenda
takeaways: Outlines key topics bridging generative AI, intelligent agent architectures, and autonomous defense systems.
Examines real-world applications, ethical challenges, and future skills required for AI-powered security.

title: Today's Cybersecurity Battlefield
takeaways: The modern cybersecurity landscape is rapidly escalating in both complexity and scale.
Critical metrics show high-frequency attacks occurring every 39 seconds and average breach costs hitting a record $4.45M.
Threat actors maintain a long presence within compromised networks, with an average of 287 days before detection.

title: AI Agents Hierarchy of Needs
takeaways: Modern cybersecurity faces systemic strain, highlighted by 5.4 billion annual malware attacks and a massive workforce shortage.
The 'Hierarchy of Needs' framework maps the stack required to build agentic systems, from base infrastructure and foundation models to specialized LLM security and observability.
Generative AI provides a critical path forward by enabling autonomous security monitoring, detection, and response to offset human talent gaps.

title: The Evolution of Cyber Threats
takeaways: Security is shifting from reactive, rule-based traditional methods to autonomous, self-improving agentic AI systems.
The evolution follows a three-stage path: Traditional (manual/reactive), AI-Enhanced (pattern detection), and Agentic (fully autonomous decision-making).

title: The New Attack Surface
takeaways: AI systems introduce new vulnerabilities through model behaviors, data exposure risks, and complex API integrations.
The interconnected nature of AI agent toolchains significantly expands the potential blast radius of security exploits.
Core security pillars—Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA)—are the primary targets within this evolving AI threat landscape.

title: Common Adversarial Tactics
takeaways: Prompt injection is the primary threat to LLMs, allowing malicious inputs to override system instructions.
Data leakage risks include the exposure of sensitive PII, internal documents, and proprietary logic by models.
Over-permissioning AI agents can transform minor security exploits into critical, system-wide failures.

title: Why Traditional Security Fails
takeaways: Conventional tools fail because AI systems are non-deterministic and dynamic, causing threats to evolve faster than traditional patch cycles.
Effective AI security requires shifting from static scanners and signature-based detection to runtime interaction monitoring, adaptive defenses, and continuous red-teaming.

title: From Chat to Action: Why Security Rules Suddenly Fail
takeaways: Agentic AI executes multi-step tasks using tools and identity with real-world side effects beyond passive text generation.
Legacy security systems fail because persistent, acting agents create entirely new attack surfaces.
Security controls must shift from simple input filtering ('prompt safety') to runtime 'workflow safety'.

title: The New Threats in the Agentic Stack
takeaways: Tool misuse occurs when agents combine valid tools into harmful workflows that bypass static security checks due to injected or ambiguous intent.
Identity and privilege abuse escalates the classic 'confused deputy' problem to machine scale via credential inheritance across task boundaries.
Dynamic trust exploitation creates fragile trust chains as agents interact with unverified dynamic tools, MCP endpoints, and other agents.

title: Multi-Agent Systems: Risk Multiplies, Observability Blinds
takeaways: Multi-agent environments introduce emergent trust boundaries where agents delegate to each other, propagating risk beyond single-agent boundaries.
System risks multiply due to cascading failures, non-deterministic emergent behaviors, and vulnerabilities in shared memory, context, and tools.
A single poisoned context can rapidly spread malicious logic across an entire agent mesh in seconds.

title: When Governance Breaks: Supply Chain & Dynamic Dependencies
takeaways: Runtime dynamic loading of tools and endpoints often lacks cryptographic verification and provenance checks.
Poisoned context and malicious logic injected into tool responses propagate silently through decision chains.
Unverified agent-to-agent delegation creates supply chain vulnerabilities without clear identity, intent, or manifest verification.

title: The Governance Shift: Static Checks → Intent + Runtime Enforcement
takeaways: AI governance is shifting away from static checks toward a model focused on intent verification and runtime enforcement.

Effective security governance relies on three nested layers: Core Intent (signed goals and verification), Runtime Controls (sandboxing and approvals), and a Standards Layer (MCP protocols and SOC integration).

title: Permission Creep via "Citizen" Agents
takeaways: Over 80% of Fortune 500 enterprises deploy AI agents without adequate governance, driving 'Shadow Agent' risks.
Autonomous agent deployment creates missing audit trails, undefined ownership, and ungoverned access permissions.
Mitigating permission creep requires Discovery, Permission Mapping, Behavioral Baselines, and Lifecycle Governance.

title: Agentic Tooling + Governance Controls Win
takeaways: Strict enforcement of MCP-based governance and tool-scoping policies resulted in an 85% reduction in unauthorized agent actions.
Implementing protocol-level verification and standards-driven orchestration achieved a 70% improvement in threat detection time.
Effective security requires constraining tool usage and treating MCP (Model Context Protocol) governance as the primary security perimeter.

title: Security as a Startup Competitive Advantage
takeaways: Startups face significant security challenges due to resource constraints, rapid deployment velocities, and complex, expanding cloud-native attack surfaces.
Lack of formal security processes often leads to inconsistent controls and audit readiness gaps.
The cost of failure is high, with 60% of small companies failing within six months following a cyber attack.

title: Automate, Codify & Build Security Culture
takeaways: Integrate security into CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure as code (IaC) to ensure auditability and reduce human error.
Prioritize practical security controls over 'security theater' and align incentives to make security a shared business value.
Cultivate a resilient organizational culture where security is seen as a competitive advantage rather than a compliance burden.

title: Real-World Example: Robin AI & Pavlov Startups
takeaways: Security readiness, such as SOC 2 and GDPR, acts as a strategic business accelerator rather than an operational bottleneck.
Proactive, founder-led security programs serve as powerful signals for both enterprise customer acquisition and investor confidence.
Integrating security from day one builds foundational trust and enables faster scaling without sacrificing innovation velocity.

title: Challenges, Ethics & Governance
takeaways: Organizations face significant risks including overreliance on AI, workforce skills gaps, and legacy infrastructure integration hurdles.
Balancing autonomous security operations with essential human oversight remains a critical governance challenge.

title: Organizational Risks
takeaways: Adopting autonomous security introduces risks including overreliance, skills gaps, and legacy infrastructure integration challenges.
Organizations must navigate the critical challenge of balancing automated AI-driven security with necessary human oversight.

title: Startup To-Do List: Foundational Controls
takeaways: Establish strict security foundations by mapping all agent-accessible tools and enforcing least-privilege credentials.
Implement human-in-the-loop oversight for high-impact actions and sanitize RAG data to secure model memory.
Ensure deployment infrastructure includes isolation, robust identity management, and continuous behavioral monitoring.

title: Designing Secure AI Systems
takeaways: Implement the principle of least privilege for all AI tool calls and API interactions.
Adopt a defense-in-depth approach by layering security guardrails and PII detection.
Ensure safe-by-design principles through modular architecture and strict component-level privilege separation.

title: A Practical Reference Model: Identity-First, Least Privilege, Telemetry
takeaways: Treat AI agents as distinct identities with full authentication and accountability rather than anonymous scripts.
Implement fine-grained, just-in-time delegation that limits tool access by task, time, and revocability.
Utilize continuous behavioral telemetry to monitor agent actions and detect deviations from established security baselines in real time.

title: Automate and Codify Security Controls
takeaways: Integrate security policies directly into version-controlled infrastructure and CI/CD pipelines to eliminate manual error and maintain velocity.
Prioritize substantive, risk-reducing controls over 'security theater' and embed incident recovery planning into the design phase.
Utilize Infrastructure as Code (IaC), automated compliance checks, and open-source security frameworks to ensure consistent, repeatable protection.

title: Build a Security Culture & Shared Responsibility
takeaways: Security must be treated as a core organizational priority involving everyone from leadership to engineering and operations teams.
Cultivating long-term resilience requires embedding security into company culture through regular training and clear communication.
Effective security strategies rely on strong leadership commitment and aligning security goals with overall business and customer objectives.

title: Student Action Plan: Learn & Build
takeaways: Develop prompt injection defense skills using interactive platforms like Lakera Gandalf.
Prioritize security by executing untrusted agent code exclusively in isolated sandboxes, away from production environments.
Deepen understanding of AI safety by studying model alignment techniques such as DPO and Constitutional AI.

title: What to Follow
takeaways: Prioritize industry-standard vulnerability references like the OWASP LLM Top 10.
Adopt emerging federal guidance such as NIST AI 100-1 for secure and resilient AI deployment.
Monitor ongoing research and safety frameworks from authoritative bodies like Berkeley RDI and Frontier Labs.

title: Your Playbook: Projects, Checklist & Career Path
takeaways: Implement hands-on capstone projects focusing on incident-response agents and agent registry prototypes to build practical expertise.
Adopt a robust governance framework that emphasizes least privilege, environment isolation, and continuous red teaming for AI agents.
Develop specialized skills in agentic threat modeling to identify and mitigate risks like tool misuse, memory poisoning, and supply chain vulnerabilities.

title: What Is Next: The Agentic Frontier
takeaways: Future AI systems will require a hybrid approach, blending symbolic and non-symbolic components to mitigate emerging architectural risks.
As AI scales beyond human oversight, implementing formal verification and provable security becomes critical for maintaining system integrity.
Security engineers must proactively adopt a strategy that combines adversarial thinking with rigorous design to ensure systems remain reliable and corrigible.

title: Emerging Trends
takeaways: The security roadmap transitions from foundational prompt engineering and orchestration toward explainable, generative adversarial systems and multi-modal cognitive frameworks by 2027.
Critical focus areas include managing agent coordination, ensuring AI ethics, and maintaining robust model evaluation to protect against emerging manipulation tactics.
